title: Restaurant email marketing for busy owners
seoTitle: Restaurant email marketing for busy owners | ROAL
description: Restaurant email marketing can bring back regulars, fill slow nights, and support phone orders. Here’s a simple plan for busy owners.
question: How should I use restaurant email marketing to bring in more orders?
answer: Restaurant email marketing works best when you send simple, local offers to people who already know your food. Collect emails from pickup orders, catering requests, and reservation follow-ups, then send short messages about specials, slow-night deals, and reminders to call or order direct. Keep it easy to read, easy to act on, and tied to real menu items.
summary: You’ll learn how to collect emails, write simple offers, and connect email marketing to phone orders and repeat business.
intro:
Restaurant email marketing works best when it is simple, local, and tied to food people already like. For most independent restaurants, the goal is not fancy design. It is getting regulars to come back, place a pickup order, or book a table.

For a busy shop, email works even better when it supports the phone. ROAL can answer calls, take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. That gives you a clean path from phone call to repeat customer, and it fits well with the basics in [How it works](/how-it-works) and [Restaurant types](/for).

sections.h2: What should restaurant email marketing do for my shop?
sections.body:
Restaurant email marketing should do three jobs: bring back regulars, fill slow hours, and keep your name top of mind. A deli, pizza shop, or family restaurant does not need long newsletters. It needs short messages that point people to one clear action.

Think in terms of one offer per email. For example: a lunch special, a family meal, a Friday pickup reminder, or a catering reminder for office groups. If your average order is $28, and a regular comes back one extra time this month, that is $28 you can trace back to the message. Plug in your own average check and your own traffic.

Use this simple test before you send anything:
- Is the offer tied to one menu item or one meal?
- Is there one action, like call, reply, or order pickup?
- Does the email fit your hours and kitchen pace?
- Can a busy customer understand it in 10 seconds?

A line you can use in the email: "Reply with your name and pickup time, and we’ll have it ready."

sections.h2: Where do I collect email addresses without slowing service?
sections.body:
The best time to collect an email is when the customer already wants something from you. That can be after a pickup order, after a reservation request, or after a catering inquiry. Do not make the front counter feel like a signup booth.

A simple collection plan:
1. Ask for an email only after the order is confirmed.
2. Add a short line to printed receipts, catering sheets, and website forms.
3. Save emails from phone orders when the caller agrees.
4. Keep one list for regulars and one for catering leads if you want different messages.

If you use a phone host like ROAL, the caller’s name and phone are already collected on the order, and staff can use that flow to build a repeat-customer list over time. The point is to keep the process natural. You want names and contact info from real orders, not random people who will never buy.

Example phone script line: "Can I also get your email for the receipt and our specials list?"

sections.h2: What should I send in a weekly restaurant email?
sections.body:
Keep the email short. One photo is enough. One offer is enough. Many owners do better with a simple format that is easy to repeat every week.

Here is a practical template:
| Part | What to write |
|---|---|
| Subject line | "Friday pickup special" |
| Opening | One sentence about the meal |
| Offer | One price or one combo |
| Timing | Lunch, dinner, or weekend |
| Action | Call, reply, or visit |

Example: say your family meal is normally $42 and you want to offer it at $38 on Tuesday and Wednesday. Put that exact number in the email, then tell people when it is available. If your own price is different, swap it in. Keep the message tied to the kitchen’s real pace so you do not overload the line.

Good email topics for restaurants:
- Lunch specials
- Slow-night deals
- Catering reminders
- Holiday preorder reminders
- New menu items
- Return-to-office office lunch offers

A short line that works: "Tuesday and Wednesday only: our family tray is ready for pickup after 4 p.m."

sections.h2: How do email and text marketing work together?
sections.body:
Email is good for detail. Text is good for urgency. Many restaurants use email for the full offer and text for the quick nudge.

Use email when you want to explain the meal, list the sides, or announce a new special. Use text when you want someone to act today. For example, an email can explain a catering tray for six people, while a text can remind the same customer that the order cutoff is in two hours.

A simple sequence:
1. Send the email with the full offer.
2. Later, send a short text to people who already opted in.
3. Keep the text shorter than the email.
4. Match the wording so customers recognize it.

Example pair:
- Email: "Our Monday pasta special is back. Call to place a pickup order before 7 p.m."
- Text: "Monday pasta special is ready. Reply or call to reserve your tray."

If your staff already handles phone orders, pair those messages with [Phone greeting templates](/tools/phone-greeting-templates) so the pickup call feels consistent from first contact to kitchen ticket.

sections.h2: How do I tie restaurant email marketing to phone orders?
sections.body:
This is where many small restaurants win. Email should not live by itself. It should point people back to the phone when that is the easiest way for them to order.

For example, a regular might open your email, see a lunch special, and call to customize it. That works especially well for pizza shops, delis, and family restaurants where customers want modifiers, notes, or a quick question answered. ROAL can take the order from the live menu, confirm the details, and send the ticket to the kitchen screen.

A practical workflow:
- Email the offer.
- Let the customer call to order.
- Keep the menu and hours current.
- Use the call history to see what people ask most.

If you want to compare channels, the math is simple. Say a delivery app keeps 15-30% of each order in commission. Say your direct phone order costs $0.90 with ROAL after the order is completed and reaches the kitchen screen. Put your own average order number next to those costs and decide which channel should carry your promotion. [Compare phone orders vs delivery apps](/compare/delivery-apps) if you want that side-by-side view.

One phone script line that fits the email: "Yes, that special is available for pickup. What size would you like?"

sections.h2: What should I track so I know if it is working?
sections.body:
Do not track ten things. Track the few that matter to a restaurant owner: opens, replies, calls, orders, and repeat visits. If you do not want a complicated system, use a basic notes sheet and your call history.

Track this each week:
- How many emails went out
- How many people replied or called
- Which menu item got the most interest
- Which day brought the most pickup orders
- Whether the offer was too big, too small, or just right

A simple example: if you email 300 people about a $19 lunch combo and 12 of them call for pickup, you can divide your own cost by 12 to estimate what each response cost you. Use your real numbers, not somebody else’s. Then compare that to what you spend on delivery apps or a monthly phone plan. Our [Pricing](/pricing) page explains how ROAL is billed monthly, with no monthly fee, setup fee, or per-minute fee.

If you want a quick calculator mindset, ask three questions after every campaign:
1. Did the phone ring more during the offer window?
2. Did orders increase on the featured day?
3. Did customers ask for the same item again later?

That is enough to improve the next email.

sections.h2: How do I keep email marketing simple when I am already busy?
sections.body:
Keep the system small enough to run during service. You do not need long copy, a designer, or a complicated schedule. You need one repeatable habit.

Try this weekly routine:
1. Pick one offer on Monday.
2. Write three sentences about it.
3. Send it to your list on the same day and time each week.
4. Use one staff member to check replies and missed questions.
5. Update your menu and hours if anything changed.

A lot of owners also use phone calls to support the email list. People who call may ask about sold-out items, hours, parking, or allergies. ROAL handles the common questions and passes tricky calls, catering requests, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests to staff with a summary. That keeps the front of house calmer when a campaign brings in extra traffic.

If you want to start without a big project, [Build a free test host](/try) from your website or Google Maps link and see how your live menu sounds on the phone. Then connect that phone flow to your email offers so customers have one clear way to order.

A final checklist:
- One offer
- One list
- One send day
- One phone number customers trust
- One clear call to action

takeaways: Send one simple offer instead of a long newsletter.
Collect emails from real orders, not random signups.
Use email for detail and text for urgency.
Tie campaigns to pickup calls, catering, or slow nights.
Track replies, calls, and orders, then adjust the next send.

faq.q: How often should a restaurant send marketing emails?
faq.a: Most independent restaurants can start with one email a week or every two weeks. The right pace is the one your team can keep up with without rushing service. If your audience is very active, you can add a text reminder for time-sensitive offers.

faq.q: What should I put in a restaurant marketing email?
faq.a: Keep it focused on one meal, one price, or one reason to call. A lunch special, family tray, catering reminder, or holiday preorder usually works better than a long list of menu items. Make the action obvious: call, reply, or place a pickup order.

faq.q: Is email better than text for restaurant promotions?
faq.a: Email is better for details, while text is better for urgency. A good approach is to send the full offer by email and then send a short text reminder to people who already opted in. That way customers get both the details and the nudge.

faq.q: How does restaurant email marketing help phone orders?
faq.a: Email can send people back to the phone when they want to customize an order, ask a question, or place a pickup request. That is useful for restaurants where customers need modifiers, timing, or quick help. When the phone is set up well, the email becomes a path to a confirmed order instead of just a message.
